name: RapidJSON
baseline: nlohmann/json (Nlohmann v2.0.3 row in nativejson-benchmark; also measured against JsonCpp, taoJSON and 40 other libraries)
workload: Parse in-memory JSON into a DOM and stringify the DOM back to condensed JSON, summed over canada.json (2199 KB), citm_catalog.json (1737 KB) and twitter.json (632 KB), default 'RapidJSON (C++)' configuration against 'Nlohmann (C++11)'.
claimed_speedup: Parse time summed over the three files: RapidJSON 7.932 ms vs Nlohmann 72.476 ms, about 9.1x faster (derived from page data; per file canada 4.755 vs 55.591 ms, citm_catalog 1.950 vs 9.875 ms, twitter 1.227 vs 7.010 ms). Stringify summed: 11.209 ms vs 87.732 ms, about 7.8x faster (derived; canada 9.338 vs 76.315, citm 1.125 vs 7.178, twitter 0.746 vs 4.239). Same CSV, strdup overhead row: parse 0.212 ms total. Insitu configuration parse total 8.114 ms; FullPrec configuration 16.454 ms (4.4x faster than Nlohmann, derived). The project's own README claims only 'RapidJSON is fast. Its performance can be comparable to strlen()' with no figures.
compiler_and_flags: clang 7.0 64-bit on macOS (README sample description). The suite's build/premake5.lua sets the release configuration to optimize 'Full' with buildoptions '-march=native -Wall -Wextra' (read from that build file, not from the results page).
stars_or_usage: 15.1k stars (page opened as miloyip/rapidjson; GitHub shows the repository as Tencent/rapidjson)
tradeoffs: Header-only with both SAX and DOM APIs; each Value is 16 bytes on most 32/64-bit machines per its README; optional SSE2/SSE4.2 acceleration. The in-situ configuration is fastest but destroys the source buffer. The default configuration does not use full-precision double parsing (the FullPrec configuration is 2x slower in the same CSV). Last tagged release is v1.1.0 from 2016-08-25.
caveats: The suite's author Milo Yip is also RapidJSON's primary author (the suite README discloses this). The sample results are dated 2016-09-09 and use Nlohmann v2.0.3, an early release; current nlohmann/json is 3.12. The numbers are DOM parse and stringify on three files, not struct mapping. Corroboration from a newer, independent run: simdjson's pinned static-reflection benchmark (GCC 16.2 -O3, Intel Xeon Gold 6548N) lists RapidJSON 0.85 GB/s vs nlohmann::json 0.15 GB/s for parsing twitter.json into structs (about 5.7x, derived), with simdjson at 5.11 GB/s, so RapidJSON is no longer the fastest. RapidJSON's own docs/performance.md only points to nativejson-benchmark and two 2013 third-party benchmarks. Lead URL miloyip/rapidjson is the old owner path of the same repository.
found_via: seed-record pass; started from the lead 'RapidJSON' at https://github.com/fffaraz/awesome-cpp#JSON (https://github.com/miloyip/rapidjson); numbers from miloyip/nativejson-benchmark sample CSV, build/premake5.lua and README (raw.githubusercontent.com); newest commit from github.com/Tencent/rapidjson/commits/master.

name: simple_enum
baseline: magic_enum v0.9.5 enum_name (also reflect::enum_name main of 2024-02-02)
workload: Template instantiation time of one enum_name call per enum, measured with clang -ftime-trace, for four bounded enums (3, 15, 40 and 104 enumerators) built from time_trace/enum_definitions.h.
claimed_speedup: README table, instantiation time simple_enum vs magic_enum: lorem_ipsum_long (104 enumerators) 12.235 ms vs 199.867 ms (about 16x, derived from page data); lorem_ipsum_short (40) 5.286 vs 178.864 ms (34x); E (15) 2.607 vs 86.089 ms (33x); strong_untyped (3) 0.830 vs 151.590 ms (183x). reflect: 19.282 ms instantiation plus 36.470 ms code generation (55.752 ms total) for the 104-enumerator enum, and 69.216 ms total for strong_untyped.
compiler_and_flags: clang 17 with -ftime-trace (README); the time_trace/CMakeLists.txt sets no optimization or language-standard options of its own.
tradeoffs: C++20 (tested up to C++23); enum_name and enum_cast need enumeration bounds: first/last members, an adl_enum_bounds function, an info<> specialization, or a default unbounded upper range (default_unbounded_upper_range). Cost is proportional to the number of enumerators for bounded enums. Also ships enum_view, enum_index, std::format and glaze integration. Initial C++ module build mode.
caveats: Measures compiler frontend cost only (instantiation time), not runtime lookup speed; the README gives no runtime benchmark. Numbers are for simple_enum v0.2.0 against magic_enum v0.9.5 (README, 2024), both since changed, and the README notes an old screenshot is from v0.0.1. Benchmark source is public (time_trace/simple_enum.cc, magic_enum.cc, reflect.cc, enum_definitions.h, CMakeLists.txt) with compiler and CPU named, so it nearly meets tier A, but optimization and standard flags and the build preset are not stated. magic_enum scans a default value range per enum while simple_enum relies on user-declared bounds, so the comparison favours the bounded case; the reflect row is not comparable per the README (part of its work moves to runtime). The lead's guessed baseline (std::string_view or manual conversion) is not what is measured.

name: Sonic-Cpp
baseline: RapidJSON (also nlohmann/json and taocpp/json in the nativejson-benchmark chart; simdjson, yyjson, cJSON and JsonCpp in the project's own benchmark)
workload: (a) Project's own Google Benchmark decode and encode of 11 JSON files (book, gsoc-2018, fgo, lottie, canada, github_events, otfcc, poet, citm_catalog, twitter, twitterescaped) against RapidJSON, yyjson and simdjson; (b) miloyip/nativejson-benchmark DOM parse and stringify of canada, citm_catalog and twitter (Time in ms, 3 files) against 30+ libraries.
claimed_speedup: No figures in the README text; numbers exist only as bar charts. Values below are read off the chart images, approximate, not printed. nativejson parse chart (docs/images/parse.png, axis 0-100 ms): Sonic about 0.9 ms vs RapidJSON about 2.1 ms (about 2.3x faster), nlohmann about 6.2 ms (about 6.9x), taocpp/json about 5.6 ms, simdjson about 0.8 ms (faster than Sonic). Serialize chart (docs/images/serialize.png, axis 0-40 ms): Sonic about 0.55 ms vs RapidJSON about 1.2 ms (about 2.2x), nlohmann about 4.6 ms (about 8x), taocpp/json about 2.65 ms, simdjson about 5.7 ms. Own decode/encode charts normalize SonicDyn to 1.0: RapidJSON decode bars span about 0.17 to 0.74 (Sonic about 1.4x to 6x faster) and encode about 0.17 to 0.64; simdjson decode about 0.76 to 1.44 and encode about 0.19 to 0.50; yyjson decode about 0.68 to 1.54 and encode about 0.40 to 1.51.
compiler_and_flags: benchmark/CMakeLists.txt compiles bench with -O3 -DNDEBUG -g plus arch flags (Google Benchmark v1.9.5); the Bazel path uses --compilation_mode=opt; compiler and version not stated.
tradeoffs: Header-only, C++11 or newer; README requires x86 with AVX2, GCC or LLVM, Linux and says MSVC is unsupported (the recent commit log mentions ARM, SVE2 and RISC-V work). Parses into a compact document tree and has an ondemand mode; SIMD whitespace skipping, string-escape search and a STOA float algorithm. The README roadmap still lists UTF-8 validation, JSON Pointer, JSON Path and RawNumber as unsupported, so it does less checking than simdjson.
caveats: Evidence is first-party and chart-only: no printed numbers, no CPU model, no compiler version, and the y-axis label 'HIB' in the decode/encode charts is undefined (read as higher is better, normalized to SonicDyn = 1.0). The nativejson-benchmark chart is a rerun by the Sonic authors on unstated hardware, with libraries of unknown versions. simdjson is faster than Sonic on the nativejson parse chart. The README's skipped UTF-8 validation makes the comparison to validating parsers (simdjson) not like-for-like. The project's own benchmark does not include nlohmann/json.

name: taoJSON
workload: Parse in-memory JSON into a DOM and stringify the DOM, summed over canada.json (2199 KB), citm_catalog.json (1737 KB) and twitter.json (632 KB), taocpp/json 1.0.0-beta.7 against Nlohmann v2.0.3.
claimed_speedup: Parse time summed over the three files: taocpp/json 41.230 ms vs Nlohmann 72.476 ms, about 1.8x faster (derived from page data; canada 25.621 vs 55.591 ms, citm_catalog 10.266 vs 9.875 ms i.e. slightly slower there, twitter 5.343 vs 7.010 ms). Stringify summed: 30.997 ms vs 87.732 ms, about 2.8x faster (derived; canada 21.560 vs 76.315, citm 6.078 vs 7.178, twitter 3.359 vs 4.239). In the same CSV RapidJSON parses the three files in 7.932 ms, so taocpp/json is about 5.2x slower than RapidJSON (derived). taoJSON's own README makes no speed claim; it says only 'Achieves a 100% conformance score in the Native JSON Benchmark tests'.
compiler_and_flags: clang 7.0 64-bit on macOS (suite README); build/premake5.lua release configuration: optimize 'Full' with '-march=native -Wall -Wextra' (read from the build file).
tradeoffs: Header-only, C++17, built on the PEGTL parsing expression grammar library; generic Value class with type traits and an events interface that converts to and from JSON, JAXN, CBOR, MsgPack and UBJSON; MIT with bundled V8 double-conversion and Ryu portions under their own licences (BSD-3 style and Apache-2.0 or BSL-1.0). Designed for flexibility and conformance rather than raw speed.
caveats: Weak, stale and contested. The project makes no performance claim; the evidence is a 2016 third-party shootout row (taocpp/json 1.0.0-beta.7 vs Nlohmann v2.0.3, run by RapidJSON's author) that predates both libraries' current releases. A later rerun of the same suite shown in the Sonic-Cpp README (chart only, hardware and versions unstated; values read off the bars, approximate) has taocpp/json parse about 5.6 ms vs Nlohmann about 6.2 ms (about 1.1x) and stringify about 2.65 vs 4.6 ms (about 1.7x), so the margin may have shrunk. An early 2019 Boost.JSON development commit (boostorg/json 7e72366) reportedly listed tao-json parse timings in the 2,000 to 23,000 ms range against nlohmann 1,297 to 13,899 ms in the same run, which would make taoJSON slower there (read from a fetch summary, not verified at source, hardware unstated). Also note taocpp/json is slower than RapidJSON in every suite found. The repo has src/perf/json benchmark programs but no published comparison numbers.

name: TinyXML2
workload: DOM parse of Wikimedia XML dumps (about 800 MB and about 1.5 GB) on Windows 10, measuring only the Parse() call for TinyXML-2, against MSXML 6.0 used through IXMLDOMDocument; part of a competitor's comparison of its own parser.
claimed_speedup: Raw parse time, TinyXML-2 vs MSXML 6.0: 800 MB 7,424,695 vs 12,940,236 microseconds (about 1.7x faster, derived from page data); 1.5 GB 12,958,705 vs 22,529,768 microseconds (about 1.7x). Load-parse-unload warm: 800 MB 9,278,020 vs 16,457,514 (1.8x), 1.5 GB 16,493,514 vs 29,422,628 (1.8x); cold 1.5 GB 20,971,263 vs 31,736,102 (1.5x). Memory at 800 MB: TinyXML-2 5477.5 MB vs MSXML 3428.5 MB. In the same tables Rapid-XML (1,686,864 microseconds at 800 MB), pugiXml (1,243,289) and mdz_xml (830,137 to 965,468) are all faster than TinyXML-2. The project's own README claims only that TinyXML-2 is 'efficient' and, against TinyXML-1, 'uses less memory, is faster, and uses far fewer memory allocations', with no figures.
compiler_and_flags: VC++ toolset v100 (64-bit); optimization flags not stated.
hardware: Intel i5-6600 @ 3.30GHz (4 cores/4 threads), 16 GB RAM, Windows 10 64-bit
tradeoffs: Small DOM parser (README: one header and one cpp file) with no dependency on the C++ standard library; UTF-8 only; its README says it was rewritten to suit use in a game (less memory, fewer allocations than TinyXML-1) and that if you need browser-level or more complete XML support 'TinyXML-2 is not the parser for you'. The README notes COLLAPSE_WHITESPACE essentially parses the document twice.
caveats: Weak evidence of an unusual kind: the numbers come from a competing commercial vendor (maxdz mdz_xml, closed source, benchmark harness not published, test files are public Wikimedia dumps from March 2021) whose tables show TinyXML-2 as the slowest of the open parsers measured (RapidXML 4.4x faster, pugiXml 6.0x faster in raw parse, derived) and crashing at 2.0 GB and 2.7 GB. Only the Parse() call was timed for TinyXML-2, other parsers include load steps in some tables. MSXML 6.0 is Windows-only, not libxml2. Other third-party data points go against it: siximapala/XML-plugins-exhibit README sample CSV (hardware unstated, Windows build instructions) has pugixml read 10 MB in 18-20 ms vs TinyXML2 65-102 ms and RapidXML 42-55 ms; libsimdxml's README says tinyxml2 errors out on its corpus and excludes it. tinyxml2 issue #52 'Benchmark?' asks for a benchmark and has no answer. The lead's guessed baseline (libxml2) has no TinyXML-2 numbers anywhere reachable.
found_via: seed-record pass; started from the lead 'TinyXML2' at https://github.com/fffaraz/awesome-cpp#XML (https://github.com/leethomason/tinyxml2); README of the repo (no numbers); numbers from maxdz-gmbh/mdz_xml README via raw.githubusercontent.com, found through a WebSearch for tinyxml2 xml parser benchmarks; commit date from github.com/leethomason/tinyxml2/commits/master.
